notes:
Task and constraints: Return each integer in `[left,right]` divisible by every decimal digit it contains; any zero digit disqualifies it.
Idea: `selfDividingNumbers` tests every candidate `x`, extracts digits with `% 10`, rejects zero or a non-divisor, and divides `n` by ten to continue.
Technique and why it applies: Digit-by-digit validation checks exactly the divisibility condition without converting numbers to strings.
Invariant: While `ok` remains true, every digit already processed is nonzero and divides the original `x`.
Edge cases: A candidate containing zero is rejected; the interval is inclusive; positive bounds are assumed by the digit loop.
Complexity: There are `right-left+1` candidates and O(log right) digits per candidate, so time is O((right-left+1) log right), with O(1) auxiliary space excluding output.
complexity_reason: The digit loop checks each decimal digit and stops as soon as a zero or non-divisor appears.

notes:
Task and constraints: List all numbers in the inclusive range divisible by each of their decimal digits, excluding numbers with a zero digit.
Idea: `selfDividingNumbers` loops over candidates, repeatedly uses `% 10` and `/= 10`, and adds only candidates whose `ok` flag stays true.
Technique and why it applies: Arithmetic digit extraction checks divisibility directly and avoids allocating a string representation for each candidate.
Invariant: `ok` is false once any processed digit is zero or fails to divide the original candidate.
Edge cases: Zero-containing numbers are rejected; `left` and `right` are inclusive; the usual positive-integer constraints are assumed.
Complexity: With R candidates and O(log right) digits each, time is O(R log right) and auxiliary space is O(1) apart from the result list.
complexity_reason: Each candidate is inspected digit by digit and rejected immediately when its rule fails.

notes:
Task and constraints: Recolor the four-directionally connected component containing `(sr,sc)` from its original color to `color`.
Idea: `floodFill` saves `old`, returns immediately if colors match, then uses a stack and recolors matching neighbors when pushing them.
Technique and why it applies: Iterative DFS explores the connected region; recoloring on discovery doubles as a visited marker and prevents repeated pushes.
Invariant: Every changed pixel belongs to the start pixel's original-color component, and every discovered pixel is already recolored.
Edge cases: If `old == color`, return without traversal; valid non-empty image and coordinates are assumed; diagonal-only contact is not connected.
Complexity: Each region pixel is processed once and checks four neighbors, giving O(mn) worst-case time and O(mn) stack space.
complexity_reason: Recoloring before pushing marks each discovered pixel so it cannot be added repeatedly.

notes:
Task and constraints: Starting from a pixel, recolor only its four-directionally connected region of the original color.
Idea: `floodFill` stores `old`, returns if it equals `color`, then uses an `ArrayDeque` stack and four direction offsets to process matching neighbors.
Technique and why it applies: Iterative flood fill reaches all and only connected pixels; changing a pixel when pushed marks it as visited.
Invariant: Pixels pushed onto `st` have the original color at discovery and are immediately changed to the new color, preventing duplicate insertion.
Edge cases: Same old and new colors require no work; the image and start coordinates are assumed valid; diagonal neighbors are ignored.
Complexity: At most four neighbor checks per image cell yield O(mn) time and O(mn) worst-case stack space.
complexity_reason: The original color is saved before recoloring, allowing the algorithm to distinguish unvisited region pixels.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the smallest letter strictly greater than `target` in a sorted array, wrapping to the first letter if none qualifies.
Idea: `nextGreatestLetter` uses a half-open binary search `[lo,hi)` to find the first letter greater than target, then wraps when `lo` reaches the length.
Technique and why it applies: Upper-bound binary search handles duplicate letters and strict comparison; wraparound is needed when every letter is at most target.
Invariant: The first qualifying index, if any, lies at or after `lo` and before `hi`.
Edge cases: Target smaller than all letters returns the first; target at or above all letters wraps; input is assumed non-empty.
Complexity: Binary search takes O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Using `<= target` to move the lower bound skips all letters that are not strictly greater.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the smallest sorted letter strictly greater than target, wrapping to the first element when necessary.
Idea: `nextGreatestLetter` searches the half-open interval `[lo,hi)` for the first element above target and returns `letters[lo % letters.length]`.
Technique and why it applies: Upper-bound search handles strict inequality and duplicates, while modulo naturally wraps an insertion point at the array length to zero.
Invariant: The candidate insertion position is the first index whose letter exceeds target, or the array length if none does.
Edge cases: A target below the minimum returns the first letter; a target at or above the maximum wraps; the array must be non-empty for modulo.
Complexity: The interval halves each iteration, giving O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The modulo expression maps the no-successor insertion point back to index zero.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the minimum accumulated stair cost to step beyond the final stair when each move advances one or two positions.
Idea: `minCostClimbingStairs` rolls two states `a` and `b` across destination indices, choosing `min(a+cost[i-2], b+cost[i-1])`.
Technique and why it applies: The cost to reach step `i` depends only on the two previous reachable steps, so earlier DP states can be discarded.
Invariant: Before each iteration, `a` and `b` are the minimum costs to reach the two consecutive positions preceding `i`.
Edge cases: The recurrence starts at position two with zero cost to start from either of the first two steps; standard input has at least two costs.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and the two rolling values use O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Only the two previous destination costs affect the next state, so the full DP array is unnecessary.

notes:
Task and constraints: Compute the minimum cost to reach beyond the last stair with one-step or two-step moves.
Idea: `minCostClimbingStairs` initializes `a` and `b` to zero and updates them with the cheaper cost from `i-2` or `i-1` for every destination index.
Technique and why it applies: The dynamic-programming recurrence depends only on the preceding two states, allowing constant-memory rolling updates.
Invariant: At the start of each loop iteration, `a` and `b` represent minimum costs to reach the previous two positions.
Edge cases: The conventional problem constraints provide at least two stair costs; the answer is the state for destination `cost.length`.
Complexity: The loop performs O(n) work and uses O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The simultaneous `next` calculation preserves both previous states until the recurrence has been evaluated.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the index of the maximum value only if it is at least twice every other value; otherwise return `-1`.
Idea: `dominantIndex` handles a singleton, finds the largest and its index, then computes the maximum of all remaining values and checks the doubled condition.
Technique and why it applies: Comparing the largest value with the runner-up is sufficient because every other value is no greater than that runner-up.
Invariant: `i` identifies a maximum element and `second` is the largest value excluding that selected occurrence.
Edge cases: A one-element array returns index zero; ties for the maximum fail the dominance condition for ordinary nonnegative inputs; the implementation assumes non-empty input.
Complexity: The maximum, index lookup, and runner-up scan are O(n) time; list slicing creates O(n) temporary space despite the stated constant-space label.
complexity_reason: The runner-up maximum determines whether the largest value dominates every other entry.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the index of the largest element if it is at least twice every other element, otherwise return `-1`.
Idea: `dominantIndex` scans once, maintaining `max`, `idx`, and `second`; a new maximum demotes the previous maximum to runner-up.
Technique and why it applies: Tracking the largest and second-largest values in one pass is enough to verify the condition against every other element.
Invariant: After each iteration, `max` and `second` are the largest and second-largest values seen, and `idx` identifies `max`.
Edge cases: A singleton returns zero; ties are handled by the `else if` branch; standard constraints assume nonnegative values, making `second=-1` a safe initial sentinel.
Complexity: The array is scanned once for O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The runner-up is updated when a former maximum is displaced or a smaller candidate exceeds it.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the shortest word that contains every license-plate letter with at least its required multiplicity, ignoring nonletters and case.
Idea: `shortestCompletingWord` builds `need` with a `Counter`, counts each candidate with `Counter(w)`, and retains the shortest candidate satisfying every frequency.
Technique and why it applies: Frequency comparison handles repeated required letters correctly, unlike a simple character-presence set.
Invariant: `ans` is the shortest completing word among candidates processed so far.
Edge cases: Nonletters in the plate are ignored; repeated letters must be matched repeatedly; the problem guarantees a completing word, otherwise this implementation returns `None`.
Complexity: For W words of average length L, counting and checking takes O(WL) time; counters use O(1) alphabet storage for the fixed English alphabet, excluding word representations.
complexity_reason: The `Counter` comparison enforces required multiplicities instead of merely checking whether each letter appears.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the shortest candidate word whose letter counts cover all letters in the license plate, ignoring case and nonletters.
Idea: `shortestCompletingWord` builds a 26-entry `need` array, creates `have` counts per word, and keeps the shortest candidate satisfying every letter count.
Technique and why it applies: Fixed-size frequency arrays compare multiplicities in constant alphabet space and naturally enforce repeated letters.
Invariant: `best` is the shortest qualifying word encountered so far; a candidate replaces it only when it is valid and shorter.
Edge cases: The plate's digits and spaces are ignored; only ASCII letters are counted; the method assumes candidate words contain lowercase English letters as in the problem constraints.
Complexity: Counting and checking all words takes O(total candidate characters + 26W), conventionally O(WL) time, with O(1) auxiliary alphabet arrays.
complexity_reason: The 26 counters represent multiplicities, so repeated license-plate letters require repeated candidate letters.

notes:
Task and constraints: Count integers in inclusive range `[left,right]` whose number of set bits is prime.
Idea: `countPrimeSetBits` uses `n.bit_count()` and checks membership in the fixed prime set `{2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19}`.
Technique and why it applies: The range bounds constrain the possible bit counts to a small finite set, making precomputed primality membership sufficient.
Invariant: The sum increments exactly for each number whose population count belongs to the prime set.
Edge cases: The inclusive endpoints are tested; counts zero and one are not prime; the listed set covers the expected integer constraints.
Complexity: Each range number is examined once, so time is O(right-left+1) under bounded integer width and auxiliary space is O(1).
complexity_reason: The fixed set contains all possible prime population counts under the problem's integer limits.

notes:
Task and constraints: Count values from `left` through `right` with a prime number of one-bits in binary form.
Idea: `countPrimeSetBits` calls `Integer.bitCount(x)` and increments `ans` only for counts explicitly listed as prime.
Technique and why it applies: Under the problem's value bounds, the number of set bits is small and the finite prime list avoids repeated primality tests.
Invariant: `ans` equals the number of qualifying integers processed so far.
Edge cases: The interval is inclusive; bit counts of zero or one are rejected; the prime constants cover the expected maximum bit count.
Complexity: The loop takes O(right-left+1) time with O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Each integer requires one bit-count operation and a constant number of comparisons against prime counts.

notes:
Task and constraints: Verify that every top-left-to-bottom-right diagonal in a matrix contains the same value.
Idea: `isToeplitzMatrix` compares each cell with `matrix[r-1][c-1]` for rows and columns starting at one.
Technique and why it applies: Equality with the upper-left neighbor propagates along each diagonal, so checking every such adjacent pair is sufficient.
Invariant: All diagonals are consistent through the cells already examined if no mismatch has been found.
Edge cases: A single row or column returns true; the code assumes a non-empty rectangular matrix.
Complexity: At most O(mn) comparisons are performed and auxiliary space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Every diagonal's equality follows from adjacent diagonal-neighbor checks across the matrix.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return true when each matrix diagonal from upper left to lower right contains equal values.
Idea: `isToeplitzMatrix` loops from row and column one onward and returns false at the first mismatch with `matrix[r-1][c-1]`.
Technique and why it applies: Matching each cell to its upper-left predecessor ensures equality propagates along every diagonal.
Invariant: If the loop continues, all adjacent pairs on every diagonal so far have matched.
Edge cases: Matrices with one row or one column are valid automatically; input is assumed non-empty and rectangular.
Complexity: The nested loops use O(mn) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The method returns immediately on the first mismatch and otherwise checks each diagonal edge once.

notes:
Task and constraints: Count each character occurrence in `stones` whose character belongs to the `jewels` string.
Idea: `numJewelsInStones` converts `jewels` to a set and sums membership booleans for every character in `stones`.
Technique and why it applies: A set gives expected constant-time membership checks, while iterating stones preserves multiplicity of repeated stone characters.
Invariant: The running sum equals the number of processed stone characters that belong to the jewel set.
Edge cases: Empty jewels yields zero; repeated stones count separately; character comparisons are case-sensitive.
Complexity: Building the set and scanning stones take O(len(jewels)+len(stones)) expected time, with O(len(jewels)) space.
complexity_reason: The set deduplicates jewel types while the stones scan still counts every matching occurrence.

notes:
Task and constraints: Count how many characters in `stones` are members of the set of jewel characters in `jewels`.
Idea: `numJewelsInStones` fills a `HashSet<Character>` from jewels, then scans every stone and increments `n` on membership.
Technique and why it applies: Hash-set lookup makes each membership test expected O(1), and repeated stone characters are counted individually.
Invariant: After each stone, `n` is the number of matching characters seen so far.
Edge cases: Empty jewel string returns zero; duplicate jewel characters do not change membership; matching is case-sensitive.
Complexity: Set construction plus stone scanning is O(J+S) expected time, and the set uses O(J) space.
complexity_reason: Each stone occurrence is tested independently, even when the same character appeared earlier.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the minimum absolute difference between values of any two distinct nodes in a BST.
Idea: `minDiffInBST` performs an in-order `dfs` into `vals`, then minimizes `b-a` over adjacent pairs using `zip(vals, vals[1:])`.
Technique and why it applies: In-order traversal of a BST yields sorted values, and the minimum difference among sorted values occurs between neighbors.
Invariant: After traversal, `vals` contains all node values in non-decreasing order.
Edge cases: The standard problem guarantees at least two nodes; duplicate values yield difference zero; a null root would make the final `min` fail.
Complexity: Traversal and adjacent comparison take O(n) time, with O(n) storage for values and recursion.
complexity_reason: Sorted in-order values reduce all-pairs comparison to adjacent differences.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the smallest difference between values of two distinct nodes in a BST.
Idea: `minDiffInBST` collects values via in-order `dfs`, then scans adjacent entries and updates `best` with `v[i]-v[i-1]`.
Technique and why it applies: BST in-order traversal sorts the values; only adjacent sorted values can form the minimum absolute difference.
Invariant: The list `v` contains every node value in sorted order after traversal.
Edge cases: The usual constraints provide at least two nodes; duplicate values yield zero; recursion depth follows tree height.
Complexity: O(n) time is needed for traversal and adjacent scan, with O(n) space for the list and recursive calls.
complexity_reason: The sorted traversal means no non-adjacent pair can have a smaller difference than its neighboring values.
